title: Steady Goes It: It's Tortoise Time
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Writing as the 2021-22 school year approaches amid "make it or break it" back-to-school pressure, Dave Stuart Jr. argues against hare-like urgency in favor of a tortoise-paced, incremental pursuit of expertise -- "today I'm going to get a bit better at this one thing." He previews three upcoming blog series (a five-key-beliefs student-motivation series with weekly practical guides, a mini-series on educator sanity built around what he calls the Workload-Pressure Paradox, and a first-ever series on the cognitive science of learning) as concrete vehicles for that steady growth. The substantive argument closes with four pointers for avoiding early-year burnout: focusing on the work that matters most rather than everything at once, keeping sight of the long-term "Everest" goal of student growth, treating mastery of material as the actual mantra of the work, and drawing communal strength from doing it together. Though structured partly as a blog-roadmap post, the piece makes a clear standalone case for incremental, unhurried professional growth as the antidote to seasonal burnout pressure.
points: Stuart explicitly rejects "make it or break it this fall" urgency in favor of incremental daily improvement, framing expertise as a tortoise-paced pursuit rather than a hare-like sprint into burnout.

The four closing pointers -- focus on the work that matters most, keep eyes on the long-term "Everest" goal, master the material as the actual mantra, and lean on communal effort -- function as a practical early-year anti-burnout checklist.
Naming the "Workload-Pressure Paradox" as a planned mini-series signals that Stuart treats educator sanity as a subject requiring sustained, structured attention, not a one-off pep talk.
The claim that focus is "competence's best accelerator" reframes single-minded prioritization, not broad effort, as the actual driver of professional growth over a school year.
quotes: But look: you and I are in the business of making long-term plans. It's never all or nothing for us. It's "Today, I'm going to get a bit better at this one thing. Tomorrow, I'll keep on that path. Bit by bit, I will progress toward expertise.
Is there a better investment in ourselves than the pursuit of expertise — of a ready knowledgeability about our work, a time-steadied gaze at the work that matters most? I don't think so.
COVID taught us a lot about the Workload-Pressure Paradox and the Journey of the Teacher's Heart. I want to spend a few weeks on practical considerations.

A lot of folks are going to drive themselves crazy this month using hare-like intensity to enter the school year on the brink of burnout. Not you and me. We know that we'll always be learning — and we're okay with that.
Focus on the work that matters most. Competence grows one day at a time; focus is its best accelerator.
Master the material. That's the mantra I've been using with my students the past few years. Mastery is fun, rewarding, communal, sweet.
